876.title: John of the Cross in prison
876.word: John of the Cross in prison
876.hook: imprisoned by his own brothers, he writes poems of love in a tiny cell, then escapes
876.howItsDone: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; Carmelites and others read his poems and his writing on the dark night, and Christians of different churches turn to them in seasons when prayer feels empty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's reform: small, poor, joyful houses on dusty roads. Your line was let nothing disturb you. What did you take out of a routine, and did it stay out? Day eight hundred seventy-six.

The cell is tiny, tradition says, little more than a closet, with light coming only through a narrow opening high in the wall. The man inside is a small, quiet friar who has been helping Teresa's reform among the men of her order. One night, friars of his own order, who opposed the reform, came and took him. Now they keep him locked in this cell in Toledo. He is brought out to be scolded, and, accounts say, beaten. He has little light, almost nothing to read, the same clothes day after day. And in the dark, he starts composing poems in his head, love poems, and memorizing them, because there's nothing to write with. Today: John of the Cross in prison.

Later, the story goes, a kinder jailer gave him a little paper and ink, and he wrote some of the poems down. Then, one night, he got out through a high window and slipped away through the streets of Toledo to a convent of Teresa's nuns, who hid him. Much of what he wrote is love poetry. Some readers hear in it an echo of the Song of Songs, where the beloved goes searching at night. In the King James Bible: "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth." One of his poems begins, in Spanish, en una noche oscura: on a dark night. A soul slips out of a quiet house, unseen, with no light to guide it except the one burning in the heart, and goes to meet the beloved. Scholars don't all agree which of his poems were made in that cell and which came later. But the shape of the prison is in them: darkness, escape, a night that turns out to be the way to love. Later he wrote long explanations of the poem, and from them comes the idea behind a phrase people still use: the dark night of the soul. In ordinary speech it has come to mean a terrible stretch. For John, the dark night is more than that. It's a time when the usual lights go out, prayer feels empty, and God, he says, is working in the dark where we can't see. A psalm says it plainly: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." The friar in the closet wrote love songs with almost no light at all.

Here's the practice: something beautiful in a hard time. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something hard right now, in your life or in the world. Don't fix it. Just let it be there. Then look, gently, for one beautiful thing inside it or beside it: a kindness, a light, a face, a small mercy. When you find it, shape it into one line, like the first line of a poem. Keep it in your head, the way John did. You can write it down after the bell. If you pray, you can offer that line to God. If you don't, just let it sit beside the hard thing. The bell holds the time.
John of the Cross in prison. A friar of Teresa's reform, locked up by his own order, who composed love poems in the dark and escaped by night.

877.title: Philip Neri
877.hook: the laughing saint of Rome, who wore his clothes inside out to stay humble
877.howItsDone: Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the Oratory communities that look back to him still gather for prayer, scripture and music; stories of his humor are often retold on his feast day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of the Cross in a tiny cell, writing poems of love, then slipping away. Your line was on a dark night. Did anything beautiful come out of a hard hour? Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

A priest is walking through the streets of Rome with half his beard shaved off. On another day, tradition says, he goes out with his clothes on inside out. People stare. Some laugh. That's the point. The man is Philip Neri, and Rome remembers him as the laughing saint. People came to him for confession and advice, and some came hoping to meet a holy man. What they found, the stories say, might be a joke, a silly hat, or a book of funny stories read aloud with a perfectly straight face. Behind all of it sat a serious question: how do you stay humble when people start calling you a saint? Today: Philip Neri.

Philip Neri lived in Rome in the age of the reformations, when the Catholic Church was working to renew itself from the inside. He didn't lead armies of preachers or write a famous book. He talked with people. He heard confessions. He gathered young men in a room to pray, read scripture, sing and talk about God, and the community that grew from those meetings came to be called the Oratory. The stories that stuck to him are mostly funny. Tradition says that when people began treating him as a living saint, he would do something ridiculous on purpose, so they'd laugh at him instead of praising him. He wasn't mocking holiness. He was guarding it. The saying linked to him is today's line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. It echoes a proverb in the King James Bible: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones." Paul says something close about giving, in his second letter to the Corinthians: "for God loveth a cheerful giver." In this way of seeing things, cheerfulness isn't a mood that shows up when life is easy. It's a strength you can lean on. A heart that can laugh at itself is harder to puff up, and harder to crush. And there's a quiet freedom in being willing to look silly. If you don't need to look impressive, your attention is free to go to other people. Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the proverb he echoes sits in the Bible Christians share.

Here's the practice: do something humbly silly. Not to perform, and never at anyone else's expense. Something small. Put your socks on mismatched. Hum a tune badly. Read a line of something out loud in a ridiculous voice, and let yourself smile. Then notice the little voice that asks, what would people think? Sit with that voice. Breathe in. Breathe out. Let it get a little smaller. If you pray, you can hold the proverb gently in mind: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine. If you don't, just rest in the lightness of not having to look impressive for a couple of minutes. The bell holds the time.
Philip Neri. A priest of Rome remembered as the laughing saint, who made himself look silly on purpose to stay humble, and who treated cheerfulness as a strength of the heart.
Your line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. Today, when something small goes wrong, try laughing at yourself first, kindly, before you fix it. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

878.title: Francis de Sales
878.hook: a gentle bishop: nothing is so strong as gentleness
878.tomorrow: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac
878.howItsDone: Catholics honor Francis de Sales as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by Christians of different churches as a guide to prayer in ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip Neri, walking through Rome with half a beard. Your line was cheerfulness strengthens the heart. Did you manage to laugh at yourself once? Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

"A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." That's a proverb from the King James Bible, and it sounds easy until someone is shouting. Then the grievous words come quickly. Today's figure is a bishop who, tradition says, had a hot temper by nature, and who spent his life learning the soft answer instead. People came to call him the gentleman saint. A saying linked to his name goes something like this: nothing is so strong as gentleness, and nothing so gentle as real strength. Today: Francis de Sales.

Francis de Sales was a Catholic priest and then a bishop, at a time when Catholics and Protestants in his corner of Europe were deeply divided. Tradition says that as a young priest he was sent into a region that had become Protestant, and that when people wouldn't come to hear him, he wrote short pages explaining his faith and slipped them under doors. Whatever you make of his arguments, notice the method: patient, quiet, personal. He wrote a book called Introduction to the Devout Life, written as letters of advice to a woman living an ordinary life in the world. Its big idea was that a life of prayer isn't only for monks and nuns. A soldier, a shopkeeper, a parent, a servant can each be devout in the life they already have, without leaving it. And the way to get there, again and again in his writing, is gentleness. Gentleness with others, yes. But also gentleness with yourself. When you fall short, he advises, don't rage at yourself. Pick yourself up the way you'd lift a friend who tripped. Harshness, in his view, just adds a second problem to the first. Paul lists gentleness among the fruit of the Spirit: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith". And Jesus, in Matthew's Gospel, describes himself this way: "for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls." Gentleness here isn't weakness. It's strength that has decided not to crush.
screen: `A DEVOUT LIFE, RIGHT WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse a gentle answer. Think of a hard conversation you're likely to have soon, or one that keeps replaying in your head. Let the other person's sharpest line arrive. Notice where it lands in your body: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Breathe out slowly. Now, without saying it aloud, try one soft answer. Not a surrender. Just a sentence with no edge on it. Then rest. If you pray, you can hold the proverb as you breathe: a soft answer turneth away wrath. If you don't, just stay with the slower breath and the unclenched jaw. The bell holds the time.
Francis de Sales. A Catholic bishop, remembered as the gentleman saint, who taught that a devout life can be lived anywhere, and that gentleness, with others and with yourself, is a kind of strength.
Your line: nothing so strong as gentleness. Today, in one hard moment, lower your voice instead of raising it, and see what happens. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

879.title: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac
879.word: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Ma
879.hook: a priest and a widow organize charity for the poor of Paris
879.howItsDone: Catholics honor Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac as saints; the Daughters of Charity and the lay Society of Saint Vincent de Paul carry on their work, and parish groups named for him run visits and food pantries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, the bishop who learned the soft answer. Your line was nothing so strong as gentleness. Where did a lower voice change a moment? Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

One Sunday in a French country parish, just before the sermon, the priest hears that a whole family nearby is sick, with no one to look after them. So he tells the congregation. That afternoon, the story goes, people stream down the road with soup and bread and blankets. Too much, all at once. Some of the food goes to waste, and by next week the family could be alone again. The priest sees the problem: kindness had shown up, but nobody had organized it. So he writes a simple plan. Who goes on which day. What they bring. How they speak to the sick. That priest was Vincent de Paul. Today: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac.

The plan grew. Groups of women in parish after parish took turns visiting the sick poor, and Vincent needed someone to hold it all together. He found her in Louise de Marillac, a widow with a sharp mind and, tradition says, a long struggle with anxiety and doubt of her own. She traveled to the groups, checked on them, trained them, and wrote to Vincent about what was working. Together they gathered young women into a community that came to be called the Daughters of Charity. These women were not to live behind convent walls. They were meant to live out among people, in hospitals, in homes, with orphans, in the streets of Paris. Vincent is remembered for putting it this way: their cloister would be the streets of the city. The reason sits in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says: "I was sick, and ye visited me". And then: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Today's line is linked to Vincent too: the poor are our masters. It flips the usual picture. The helper isn't the one in charge. The people being served are the ones to be honored, listened to, waited on, the way a good servant attends to a household. Catholics honor both as saints, and the Daughters of Charity still serve today.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one hour of service. Not a vague someday, an actual hour. In the quiet, think of who near you needs help: a food bank, a shelter, a neighbor who's sick, someone at a care home who rarely gets visitors. Pick one. Then do what Vincent did and make it concrete: which day, what time, what you'd bring. When the plan is set, let it go and just breathe. If you pray, you can rest with the words: I was sick, and ye visited me. If you don't, rest with the face of the person you'll serve. The bell holds the time.
Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac. A priest and a widow who turned scattered kindness into organized care for the poor of Paris, and sent women out to serve in the streets.
screen: `VINCENT DE PAUL AND LOUISE DE MARILLAC — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the poor are our masters. Today, put your hour of service on the calendar, with a day and a time, so it stops being a good intention. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: St Bartholomew's Day (1572)
880.hook: Protestants killed in Paris; religion used for massacre
880.howItsDone: Christians of different churches remember the massacre in histories, sermons and services of repentance and reconciliation, and pray for places where religion is used to justify violence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac, turning scattered kindness into a plan. Your line was the poor are our masters. Did your hour of service find a day? Day eight hundred eighty.

It begins with a wedding. In Paris, the Catholic king's sister marries the Protestant king of Navarre, and the match is meant to help end years of fighting between French Catholics and French Protestants, who were called Huguenots. Protestant nobles come to the city for the celebration. Soon after, on the feast of the apostle Bartholomew, the killing starts. First the Huguenot leaders. Then neighbors turn on neighbors in the streets, and the violence spreads beyond Paris to other towns. A day on the church calendar, named for one of the twelve, becomes the name of a massacre. This is a hard lesson, and an honest one. Today: St Bartholomew's Day.

Historians still argue about who gave the orders, and how much was planned and how much was a mob let loose. What isn't in doubt is that people were killed for their faith by other people who said they shared the same Lord. In the wars of religion that tore at France, both Catholics and Protestants killed, and both were killed. St Bartholomew's Day is the one whose name stuck. So it's worth going back to the Gospels, because this exact temptation shows up there. In Luke, Jesus and his friends are turned away by a Samaritan village. Two of the disciples, James and John, ask if they should call down fire from heaven to destroy it. Jesus doesn't take the offer. In the King James Bible: "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of." And on the night of his arrest, when one of his followers draws a sword to defend him (John's Gospel names him as Peter), Jesus says, in Matthew: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Those are his own followers, reaching for violence on his behalf, and both times he says no. That's where today's line comes from: never in his name. It's not a line about other people's faiths. It's a line Christians can turn on their own story, honestly, without pretending it didn't happen. Remembering a day like this isn't about blame across the centuries. It's about recognizing the moment a faith starts to be used as a weapon, so the sword goes back in its place.
screen: `KILLED BY THOSE WHO SHARED THEIR LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the places where religion is being used for violence. Bring one to mind, near or far, in the news or in history. Don't try to sort out who's to blame. Just hold the people: the ones who are afraid tonight, the ones grieving, and even the ones holding the weapons. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can pray for that place in your own words, or rest with the line: put up again thy sword into his place. If you don't, simply keep that place in your attention, with care, for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
St Bartholomew's Day. The feast day in Paris when Protestants were massacred, and a name that has come to stand for faith used as a weapon.
Your line: never in his name. Today, when you hear faith used to justify hurting someone, notice it, and name it quietly to yourself for what it is. Day eight hundred eighty.

881.title: The Thirty Years' War
881.hook: Europe tears itself apart until the Peace of Westphalia
881.howItsDone: Christians in different churches pray for places at war in their services and at home, and the beatitude 'blessed are the peacemakers' is one they may read when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Bartholomew's Day, a wedding that ended in a massacre. Your line was never in his name. Did you hear faith used as a weapon, and name it? Day eight hundred eighty-one.

In Prague, an angry crowd of Protestant nobles storms into a castle room, grabs royal officials, and throws them out of a high window. The officials survive the fall. The story goes that Catholics said angels had caught them, while their enemies said they'd landed in a heap of dung. Either way, nobody laughed for long. That window opened onto a war that would grind on and on, fought across German lands by armies that came and went and came back again, Catholic and Protestant rulers on both sides, and plenty of soldiers who fought mainly for pay. Today: The Thirty Years' War.

It started as a quarrel about religion and rights in Bohemia. It didn't stay there. Kings and princes joined in for faith, for land, for power, and before long the lines blurred. Catholic France ended up backing Protestant armies against the Catholic Habsburgs. The religious labels stayed on the banners, but the reasons kept multiplying. And the kings were not the ones who paid. Villagers did, in the path of armies that lived off the land, taking food, burning farms, spreading hunger and sickness behind them. Then, slowly, came the end. Diplomats gathered in two towns in Westphalia, in northwest Germany, Catholics in one and Protestants in the other, and the talks dragged on and on. Out of them came the Peace of Westphalia. It didn't make anyone agree about God. What it did was set terms for living side by side: Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed rulers were all recognized, and Europe began, unevenly, to step back from fighting wars over which church was right. Peace at last, but a tired peace, bought at a terrible cost. The prophet Isaiah describes a different kind of ending, in the King James Bible: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Westphalia wasn't that. Treaties never quite are. But it was a step back from the edge. And Jesus' words sit beside any peace table: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

Here's the practice: hold a war-torn region, and its peacemakers. Choose one place where fighting hasn't ended, today. This time, look for the people working to stop it: a negotiator at a long table, a medic, a neighbor sharing bread across a line, someone carrying messages between two sides. Breathe in, and let one of them come close. Breathe out, and wish them strength for the slow work. If you pray, you can pray for that region and its peacemakers in your own words, or rest with Jesus' line: blessed are the peacemakers. If you don't, keep those people in your attention, and wish their place peace at last. The bell holds the time.

The Thirty Years' War. A war that began over religion in central Europe, spread into a struggle for power, and ended with the Peace of Westphalia, which let Catholic and Protestant rulers live side by side.
Your line: peace at last. Today, find one small conflict in your own life that has dragged on too long, and take one step toward ending it, even a tired one. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

882.title: The King James Bible (1611)
882.hook: scholars working in companies produce an English Bible whose phrases are still in the language
882.carry: the language of heaven, in english
882.howItsDone: Some churches read the King James Version in every service, while others use newer translations and keep the King James for familiar passages such as Psalm 23, read at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Thirty Years' War, and a tired treaty in Westphalia. Your line was peace at last. Did one long quarrel take a step toward ending? Day eight hundred eighty-two.

The salt of the earth. A law unto themselves. The powers that be. Fight the good fight. The skin of my teeth. People say these without a second thought, at work, in sports commentary, in arguments about politics. Every one of them sits, word for word, in the same old book. Open it to the book of Job, and there's a man who has lost nearly everything, saying: "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth." The book is an English Bible made at the order of a king, and its sound has hung around in the language ever since. Today: The King James Bible.

King James ruled England and Scotland at a time when English Christians were reading more than one translation, and arguing about them. So a new one was ordered, to be read aloud in churches. Teams of scholars were set to work, in groups that took different parts of the Bible, and their drafts were checked and revised together. Its title page says it was translated out of the original tongues, with the former translations diligently compared and revised. That last part matters. The translators didn't start from nothing. They leaned on English Bibles that came before, including the work of William Tyndale, who had been executed as a heretic. Their preface, written to the reader, uses a string of pictures for what translation does: it opens a window to let in the light, it breaks the shell so we can eat the kernel, it pulls back the curtain. And the result was made for the ear. Listen to the opening of the twenty-third Psalm: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." Short words. A steady beat. Words to be said out loud in a stone church. Today some Christians still read the King James as their main Bible, and others treasure it alongside newer translations. Either way, its rhythm is why today's line fits: the language of heaven, in english.
screen: `A NEW TRANSLATION, ORDERED BY A KING.`
`A WINDOW TO LET IN THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a King James psalm aloud. Psalm twenty-three is a good place to start. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find it. If not, use the lines from today: the LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. Read slowly, at a speaking volume, as if to a room. Let the short words land one at a time. Then stop, and sit with the sound still in the air. If you pray, you can let the psalm become your prayer. If you don't, just notice the rhythm, and what it does to your breath. The bell holds the time.
The King James Bible. An English Bible made at a king's order to be read aloud in churches, translated from the original tongues with earlier English versions compared, and written for the ear.
Your line: the language of heaven, in english. Today, listen for one Bible phrase that turns up in ordinary talk, and notice where it came from. Day eight hundred eighty-two.
